Let’s dive into Chapter 9: Overcoming Obstacles and the Temptation of Bad Strategy.
So, you’ve got a solid strategy in place, but have you ever noticed how real progress still gets tripped up by unexpected roadblocks?
Every organization faces challenges—some come from within, others from the outside world. Recognizing these hurdles and figuring out how to move past them? That’s where the real work begins.
Let’s talk about a few obstacles that show up time and again.
First, there’s organizational inertia. You know those old routines and habits that just seem to stick, even when everyone agrees it’s time for a change? It’s like trying to steer a massive ship—it takes real effort to change course.
Then, there’s the challenge of resource constraints. Sometimes, there just isn’t enough time, money, or talent to do everything you want. That means making tough choices about what really matters.
Don’t forget about political resistance. Not everyone’s going to love the new direction. Some people might even work against it, whether it’s out of fear, self-interest, or just a difference in perspective.
And finally, there’s the pressure of the short-term. Quarterly results, urgent crises, or just the noise of day-to-day business can easily pull focus away from those long-term goals that actually move the needle.
So, how do you get past these barriers?
One of the smartest things you can do is communicate the why. Show people the logic behind your strategy—help them see how it solves a real problem.
Next, look for early wins. These are quick, visible successes that make people believe the strategy is already working. They build momentum and make it easier to tackle bigger challenges down the road.
You’ll also want to align incentives. Make sure that the rewards and recognition actually support the behaviors and outcomes you’re after. If the incentive system sends mixed messages, old habits will win every time.
And above all, stay the course. Adjust your tactics when you need to, but don’t give up on your strategy just because things get tough. Real change takes time—and a bit of persistence goes a long way.
But here’s something else to watch out for—the return of bad strategy. It’s tempting, isn’t it? Easy answers, vague goals, plans that sound good but don’t mean much. To keep your strategy sharp, revisit it often. Ask yourself: Is our diagnosis still accurate? Are our policies and actions still focused and coherent?
Think of strategy as tending a garden. It needs regular care and attention. You’ve got to weed out distractions, nurture the conditions for growth, and keep an eye out for anything that doesn’t belong. Left alone, those weeds—old habits, wishful thinking, outdated routines—can quickly take over.
So, keep your strategy alive and thriving by facing obstacles head-on, resisting the pull of easy fixes, and giving your plan the ongoing care it needs.
